# Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal

Aojie Yuan Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles,
CA, USA    Zhiyuan Julian Su Affiliation: University of Southern
California, Los Angeles, CA, USA    Haiyue Zhang Affiliation: University
of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA    Yi Nian
Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA   
Yue Zhao Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles,
CA, USA

###### Abstract

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting assumes that generated reasoning
reflects a model’s internal computation. We show this assumption is
wrong in a specific, measurable way: _models internally detect their own
reasoning errors but outwardly express confidence in them_. A linear
probe on hidden states predicts trace correctness with 0.95 AUROC—from
the _very first reasoning step_ (0.79)—while verbalized confidence for
wrong traces is 4.55/5, nearly identical to correct ones (4.87/5). A
text-surface classifier achieves only 0.59 on the same data, confirming
a 0.20-point gap invisible in the generated text. This _hidden error
awareness_ holds across three model families (Qwen, Llama, Phi),
1.5B–72B parameters, and RL-trained reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, 0.852
AUROC).

The natural question is whether this signal can fix the errors it
detects. It cannot. Four interventions—activation steering, probe-guided
best-of-N, self-correction, and activation patching—all fail; patching
_destroys_ output coherence entirely. The signal is diagnostic, not
causal: a readout of computation quality, not a lever to redirect it.
This delineates a boundary for mechanistic interpretability: error
representations during reasoning are fundamentally different from the
factual knowledge representations that prior work has successfully
edited.

## 1 Introduction

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib1)) rests
on an implicit contract: the model’s written reasoning reflects its
internal computation. If the text says “$`3\times 5=15`$,” the model
computed this and will build on it. Prior work has questioned this
contract through behavioral tests—showing that CoT explanations can be
steered by irrelevant cues ([Turpin et al., 2023](#bib.bib2)) or
truncated without changing the answer ([Lanham et al.,
2023](#bib.bib3))—but these interventions operate on the text surface. A
direct comparison between what models _say_ and what they _internally
represent_ during reasoning has been missing.

We provide this comparison by training linear probes on hidden states
extracted during CoT generation
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Contributions. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")).
The results tell a story in three acts, each raising the stakes of the
previous finding.

Act I: The signal exists, and it is early. A logistic regression probe
achieves 0.95 AUROC for predicting trace correctness—far exceeding
verbalized confidence (0.67), self-consistency (0.82), and CCS ([Burns
et al., 2023](#bib.bib4)) (0.72). The signal is present from the very
first reasoning step (0.79 AUROC), before any error appears in text
(§[3](#S3 "3 The Error Signal Exists ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")).

Act II: The model conceals what it knows. Wrong traces express
confidence of 4.55/5 (correct: 4.87/5). A text classifier on the same
first step achieves only 0.59 AUROC—a 0.20 gap confirming genuine
concealment. Fully 65% of wrong traces fall in an _unfaithful region_:
high confidence _and_ high internal error score
(§[4](#S4 "4 The Signal Is Early and Hidden ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")).

Act III: The signal cannot fix the errors it detects. Four intervention
strategies all fail
(§[5](#S5 "5 The Signal Cannot Fix What It Detects ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")).
Activation patching of correct hidden states into wrong traces destroys
output coherence (accuracy $`\to 0\%`$), revealing that the error signal
is a diagnostic readout, not a causal lever—in stark contrast to factual
knowledge representations ([Meng et al., 2022](#bib.bib10)), which can
be localized and edited.

#### Contributions.

(1) We identify _hidden error awareness_—a 0.20 AUROC gap between
hidden-state and text-surface detection—robust across 9 models
(1.5B–72B), three families, and RL-trained reasoning models. (2) We
establish the _diagnostic–causal distinction_ via four interventions,
demonstrating that error signals occupy a fundamentally different role
than factual knowledge representations. (3) We characterize two temporal
regimes of error encoding (_front-loaded_ vs. _accumulating_), providing
mechanistic insight into how models commit to flawed trajectories.

![Refer to caption](2605.09502v1/figures/rar_figure1.png)

Figure 1: Overview. (1. Hidden State Probing) A linear probe achieves
0.95 AUROC; verbalized confidence is uninformative. (2. Textual
Indistinguishability) First-step probe (0.79) vs. text classifier
(0.59): a 0.20 gap invisible on the surface. (3. Intervention
Failure) Four interventions fail; the signal is diagnostic, not causal.

## 2 Related Work

#### CoT faithfulness.

[Turpin et al. (2023)](#bib.bib2) show that CoT explanations can be
steered by irrelevant features, and [Lanham et al. (2023)](#bib.bib3)
find that perturbing CoT steps often does not change the answer. These
studies diagnose unfaithfulness via _behavioral_ interventions. We
provide a complementary _representational_ perspective: directly
comparing what hidden states encode with what the text expresses, and
quantifying the gap.

#### Probing internal representations.

[Burns et al. (2023)](#bib.bib4) discover “truth directions” via
unsupervised CCS; [Azaria and Mitchell (2023)](#bib.bib12) train
classifiers to detect falsehoods; [Li et al. (2023)](#bib.bib5) use
probes for inference-time intervention. Concurrent work by [Zhang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib14) probes hidden states in reasoning models for
self-verification, demonstrating best-of-N selection. Our work reaches a
fundamentally different conclusion: where they show the signal aids
_selection_, we show it cannot improve _the reasoning itself_. We
further establish a 0.20 AUROC gap between hidden-state and text-surface
classifiers that verification-focused work does not measure.

#### Self-correction and causal analysis.

[Huang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7) find that intrinsic self-correction
remains limited. Our activation patching experiments extend causal
mediation analysis ([Meng et al., 2022](#bib.bib10); [Vig et al.,
2020](#bib.bib11)) from factual recall to multi-step reasoning,
revealing that the causal structure of error representations differs
qualitatively from that of factual associations.

## 3 The Error Signal Exists

### 3.1 Method

Given a model $`\mathcal{M}`$ with $`L`$ layers, we extract the hidden
state $`\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ at layer $`l`$ and the
last token position $`T`$ of a complete CoT trace. We train a logistic
regression probe:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
p(\text{error}\mid\mathbf{h})=\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{h}+b)
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathbf{h}`$ is standardized (zero mean, unit variance per
dimension) and the label $`y=1`$ if the trace reaches an incorrect
answer. The training objective is regularized log-likelihood:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[y_{i}\log\hat{p}_{i}+(1{-}y_{i})\log(1{-}\hat{p}_{i})\right]+\frac{1}{2C}\|\mathbf{w}\|^{2}
``` |  | (2) |

with $`C=0.1`$. Training uses 100 MATH-500 problems ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib9)), disjoint from all evaluation sets. We select the best
layer by 5-fold cross-validated AUROC; no other hyperparameters are
tuned.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Method ‣ 3 The Error Signal Exists ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")
summarizes the full pipeline.

0:  Model $`\mathcal{M}`$, training set $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}`$,
candidate layers $`\mathcal{L}`$

0:  Best probe $`(f^{*},l^{*})`$

1:  for each problem $`x_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}`$ do

2:   $`r_{i}\leftarrow\text{GenerateCoT}(\mathcal{M},x_{i})`$ // greedy

3:
  $`y_{i}\leftarrow\mathbf{1}[\text{answer}(r_{i})\neq\text{ref}(x_{i})]`$

4:   for each layer $`l\in\mathcal{L}`$ do

5:
   $`\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{i}\leftarrow\text{ExtractHidden}(\mathcal{M},x_{i}\oplus r_{i},l)`$

6:   end for

7:  end for

8:  for each layer $`l\in\mathcal{L}`$ do

9:
  $`\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\leftarrow\text{Standardize}([\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{N}])`$

10:
  $`a_{l}\leftarrow\text{CV-AUROC}(\text{LogReg}(\mathbf{X}^{(l)},\mathbf{y}),k{=}5)`$

11:  end for

12:  $`l^{*}\leftarrow\arg\max_{l}a_{l}`$

13:  $`f^{*}\leftarrow\text{LogReg}(\mathbf{X}^{(l^{*})},\mathbf{y})`$
// fit on all data

14:  return $`(f^{*},l^{*})`$

Algorithm 1 Hidden Error Awareness Probe

### 3.2 Results across models and scales

Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Results across models and scales ‣ 3 The Error Signal Exists ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")
shows that the probe achieves $`>`$0.9 AUROC for five of nine
models—including at 72B scale (0.977). The signal is weaker at
intermediate scales (7B: 0.669, 14B: 0.762) but recovers at 32B and 72B,
suggesting the dip reflects training dynamics rather than a scaling
limitation
(§[7](#S7 "7 Discussion ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")).
The RL-distilled reasoning model DeepSeek-R1-7B also shows strong hidden
error awareness (0.852), despite 76% base accuracy.

#### Comparison with baselines.

Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Comparison with baselines. ‣ 3.2 Results across models and scales ‣ 3 The Error Signal Exists ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")
compares the probe against established detection methods on 200 held-out
problems. The probe outperforms all baselines at minimal cost, including
self-consistency (5$`\times`$ generation cost) and CCS (same hidden
states, unsupervised). The signal is linearly encoded: a linear probe
(0.955) matches an MLP (0.944) and exceeds a random forest (0.893). It
is also data-efficient: 20 training problems yield 0.956 AUROC.

| Method                                | AUROC | Cost            |
|---------------------------------------|-------|-----------------|
| Hidden State Probe (ours)             | 0.953 | 1 fwd pass      |
| Self-Consistency ($`N`$=5)            | 0.823 | 5$`\times`$ gen |
| CCS ([Burns et al., 2023](#bib.bib4)) | 0.718 | 1 fwd pass      |
| $`P`$(True)                           | 0.721 | 1 query         |
| Verbalized Confidence                 | 0.674 | 1 query         |
| Sequence Log-prob                     | 0.676 | free            |

Table 2: Error detection baselines (Qwen2.5-3B, $`n`$=200).

#### Difficulty control.

A key concern is confounding with problem difficulty. For 50 problems,
we generate 5 traces each (temperature $`=0.7`$) and compare probe
scores for correct vs. wrong traces *on the same problem*
(Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Difficulty control. ‣ 3.2 Results across models and scales ‣ 3 The Error Signal Exists ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")).
Wrong traces score significantly higher ($`p<0.05`$,
$`d=0.55`$–$`0.83`$), confirming trace-level detection.

| Model        | Mixed | Correct | Wrong | $`d`$ |
|--------------|-------|---------|-------|-------|
| Qwen2.5-3B   | 18    | 0.278   | 0.481 | 0.55  |
| Qwen2.5-7B   | 13    | 0.154   | 0.391 | 0.63  |
| Qwen2.5-14B  | 18    | 0.454   | 0.502 | 0.13  |
| Llama-3.1-8B | 24    | 0.363   | 0.561 | 0.69  |

Table 3: Within-problem difficulty control. Mixed = problems with both
correct and wrong traces; $`d`$ = Cohen’s $`d`$.

#### Layer analysis.

Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Layer analysis. ‣ 3.2 Results across models and scales ‣ 3 The Error Signal Exists ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")
shows the error signal concentrates in the upper layers (70–85% depth),
suggesting encoding in abstract, higher-level representations rather
than early syntactic processing.

Figure 2: Probe AUROC across layers. The error signal peaks in the upper
third of the network across all model families.

## 4 The Signal Is Early and Hidden

### 4.1 First-step prediction

The first-step hidden state alone achieves 0.787 AUROC—98% of full-trace
performance
(Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.1 First-step prediction ‣ 4 The Signal Is Early and Hidden ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")).
For DS-R1-7B, first-step AUROC is 0.686, still well above chance. The
model “knows” from Step 1 whether its reasoning will succeed, yet
proceeds to generate multiple incorrect steps.

| Hidden State Used       | AUROC | 95% CI           |
|-------------------------|-------|------------------|
| First step only         | 0.787 | \[0.634, 0.840\] |
| Last step only          | 0.754 | –                |
| Max score across steps  | 0.800 | \[0.696, 0.883\] |
| Mean score across steps | 0.827 | –                |
| Full trace (last token) | 0.800 | –                |

Table 4: AUROC from different trace positions (Qwen2.5-3B, $`n`$=89).
The first step captures 98% of full-trace performance.

#### Two temporal regimes.

Step-level probe scores
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Two temporal regimes. ‣ 4.1 First-step prediction ‣ 4 The Signal Is Early and Hidden ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal"))
reveal distinct dynamics. Qwen2.5-3B shows *front-loaded* awareness:
maximum separation at Step 1 (gap = 0.41), suggesting early commitment
to a flawed trajectory. Qwen2.5-7B shows *accumulating* awareness:
separation grows from 0.11 to 0.38 as error evidence builds. Neither
pattern is consistent with the probe merely reading post-hoc text
quality.

Figure 3: Step-level probe trajectories. 3B (left): front-loaded—the
model commits early. 7B (right): accumulating—error signals build
through the trace.

### 4.2 Textual indistinguishability

If the signal is in hidden states, is it also in the text? We formalize
this with a *textual indistinguishability test*: train a TF-IDF +
logistic regression classifier on first-step *text* and compare with the
hidden-state probe.

Let $`s_{\text{text}}`$ and $`s_{\text{hidden}}`$ denote the AUROC of
the text and hidden-state classifiers, respectively. We define the
*concealment gap*:

|     |                                                           |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta_{\text{conceal}}=s_{\text{hidden}}-s_{\text{text}}
       ```                                                        |     | (3) |

A positive $`\Delta_{\text{conceal}}`$ indicates information present in
hidden states but absent from text.
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.2 Textual indistinguishability ‣ 4 The Signal Is Early and Hidden ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal"):
$`\Delta_{\text{conceal}}=0.197`$, with no significant surface
differences (length $`p=0.211`$, number density $`p=0.726`$, $`<`$1%
hedging).

|                                           |           |             |
|-------------------------------------------|-----------|-------------|
| Signal                                    | AUROC     | $`p`$-value |
| TF-IDF + LR (text)                        | 0.590     | –           |
| Hidden-state probe                        | 0.787     | –           |
| *Surface statistics (correct vs. wrong):* |           |             |
| Length (tokens)                           | –         | $`p=0.211`$ |
| Number density                            | –         | $`p=0.726`$ |
| Hedging language                          | 0% vs. 1% | –           |
| Vocab. Jaccard                            | 0.322     | –           |

Table 5: Textual indistinguishability (Qwen2.5-3B, $`n`$=200).
$`\Delta_{\text{conceal}}=0.197`$.

### 4.3 The unfaithful region

We define a trace as *unfaithful* when it simultaneously exhibits high
verbalized confidence ($`\geq 4`$) and high probe error score
($`>0.5`$). Fully 65% of wrong traces fall in this region.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 The unfaithful region ‣ 4 The Signal Is Early and Hidden ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")
visualizes the separation: probe scores cleanly distinguish correct from
wrong traces, while verbalized confidence does not.

Figure 4: Probe score distributions for correct (green) vs. wrong (red)
traces. The distributions are well-separated in hidden-state space
despite near-identical verbalized confidence (4.87 vs. 4.55 out of 5).

## 5 The Signal Cannot Fix What It Detects

If models internally detect errors, can we leverage this for
self-improvement? We test four strategies spanning the intervention
spectrum and find that none meaningfully improve accuracy.

### 5.1 Activation steering

Following [Zou et al. (2023)](#bib.bib6), we define the *error
direction* $`\hat{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{w}/\|\mathbf{w}\|`$ from the probe
weight vector and subtract it during generation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{h}^{\prime}=\mathbf{h}-\alpha\cdot(\mathbf{h}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{w}})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{w}}
``` |  | (4) |

The intuition: if error is a direction in representation space, removing
it should yield “correct reasoning.”
Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.1 Activation steering ‣ 5 The Signal Cannot Fix What It Detects ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal"):
at most $`+4\%`$ improvement; aggressive steering ($`\alpha=8`$)
degrades the 3B model by $`-6\%`$. The error direction and the “correct
reasoning” direction are not opposites.

|            |     |            |     |            |
|------------|-----|------------|-----|------------|
|            | 3B  |            | 7B  |            |
| $`\alpha`$ | Acc | $`\Delta`$ | Acc | $`\Delta`$ |
| 0          | .53 | –          | .60 | –          |
| 0.5        | .56 | +.03       | .60 | .00        |
| 1.0        | .55 | +.02       | .61 | +.01       |
| 2.0        | .55 | +.02       | .62 | +.02       |
| 5.0        | .56 | +.03       | .60 | .00        |
| 8.0        | .47 | $`-.06`$   | .64 | +.04       |

Table 6: Activation steering. Gains are modest; aggressive steering
degrades the smaller model.

### 5.2 Probe-guided best-of-N

We generate $`N`$ traces (temperature $`=0.7`$) and select by lowest
probe score:

|     |                                                     |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r^{*}=\arg\min_{r\in\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{N}\}}f^{*}(r)
       ```                                                  |     | (5) |

Table [7](#S5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 5.2 Probe-guided best-of-N ‣ 5 The Signal Cannot Fix What It Detects ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal"):
probe selection matches random and substantially underperforms majority
vote. The oracle upper bound (88–91% at $`N`$=12) confirms correct
traces exist—the bottleneck is selection quality.

|              |        |        |     |       |        |
|--------------|--------|--------|-----|-------|--------|
| $`N`$        | Greedy | Random | MV  | Probe | Oracle |
| *Qwen2.5-3B* |        |        |     |       |        |
| 3            | .60    | .59    | .63 | .58   | .73    |
| 8            | .60    | .60    | .67 | .63   | .84    |
| 12           | .60    | .56    | .75 | .62   | .88    |
| *Qwen2.5-7B* |        |        |     |       |        |
| 3            | .70    | .71    | .71 | .71   | .84    |
| 8            | .70    | .70    | .76 | .73   | .91    |
| 12           | .70    | .72    | .75 | .70   | .91    |

Table 7: Probe-guided best-of-N. MV = majority vote. Despite large
oracle headroom, the probe cannot outperform majority vote.

### 5.3 Self-correction

We use the probe to flag likely errors ($`f^{*}(r)>\tau`$), then prompt
the model to revise.
Table [8](#S5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 5.3 Self-correction ‣ 5 The Signal Cannot Fix What It Detects ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal"):
retry *hurts* accuracy ($`-3\%`$). Even oracle-triggered correction
gains only $`+1\%`$. The model generates its correction using the same
flawed computation that produced the original error.

| Strategy            | 3B              | 7B              |
|---------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Greedy (no retry)   | 0.60            | 0.70            |
| Always retry        | 0.57 ($`-3\%`$) | 0.67 ($`-3\%`$) |
| Best-of-two (probe) | 0.60            | 0.70            |
| Oracle-triggered    | 0.61 ($`+1\%`$) | 0.71 ($`+1\%`$) |

Table 8: Self-correction. Retry degrades accuracy; even an oracle
trigger gains only $`+1\%`$.

### 5.4 Activation patching: the causal test

The strongest test of causality. For mixed-outcome problems, we extract
hidden states from a correct trace and patch them into a new generation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{h}^{\prime}_{\text{wrong}}=(1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{h}_{\text{wrong}}+\alpha\,\mathbf{h}_{\text{correct}}
``` |  | (6) |

If the error signal is causal, patching should improve accuracy.
Table [9](#S5.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 5.4 Activation patching: the causal test ‣ 5 The Signal Cannot Fix What It Detects ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal"):
it does not. At $`\alpha=0.5`$, 3B accuracy drops to 0%—the patched
states are incompatible with surrounding computation.

| Patching Method                 | 3B   | 7B   |
|---------------------------------|------|------|
| Baseline (no patch)             | 0.65 | 0.33 |
| Replace with correct HS         | 0.35 | 0.33 |
| Blend ($`\alpha`$=0.3)          | 0.52 | 0.20 |
| Blend ($`\alpha`$=0.5)          | 0.00 | 0.07 |
| Subtract error ($`\alpha`$=0.5) | 0.65 | 0.47 |
| Subtract error ($`\alpha`$=2.0) | 0.61 | 0.47 |

Table 9: Activation patching on mixed-outcome problems. Replacing or
blending destroys accuracy; the error direction is not a causal lever.

These four experiments converge on a single conclusion: the error signal
is a diagnostic readout—a summary statistic of computation quality—not a
causal component that can be edited to redirect reasoning.
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.4 Activation patching: the causal test ‣ 5 The Signal Cannot Fix What It Detects ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")
summarizes the results.

Figure 5: Intervention summary. (a) Steering: marginal gains,
degradation at high $`\alpha`$. (b) Best-of-N: probe underperforms
majority vote despite large oracle headroom. (c) Self-correction: retry
hurts both models.

## 6 Does RL Training Close the Gap?

DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B achieves 76% accuracy (vs. 46% for
Llama-3.1-8B) but still exhibits 0.852 AUROC hidden error awareness
(Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Results across models and scales ‣ 3 The Error Signal Exists ‣ Hidden Error Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning:The Signal Is Diagnostic, Not Causal")).
Its first-step AUROC (0.686) is lower than Qwen-3B’s (0.787), consistent
with reasoning models distributing computation across longer traces.

The difficulty control effect is weaker ($`p=0.447`$, $`d=-0.30`$),
likely because 76% accuracy leaves too few mixed-outcome problems
($`n`$=14). But the core finding stands: RL training does not close the
diagnostic–causal gap.

## 7 Discussion

#### Why diagnostic but not causal?

The thermometer analogy: a thermometer reads body temperature but cannot
cure fever. The probe reads computation quality but cannot redirect
reasoning. Patching provides the strongest evidence: transplanting
hidden states from correct traces does not produce correct reasoning—it
produces incoherent output. Reasoning quality emerges from distributed,
multi-layer computation, not from a single editable feature.

#### Contrast with factual editing.

[Meng et al. (2022)](#bib.bib10) and [Li et al. (2023)](#bib.bib5) edit
localized representations to reliably change outputs. Error signals
during reasoning are different: they are *epiphenomenal readouts* of a
distributed process. The tools that work for factual knowledge (ROME,
ITI) should not be expected to work for reasoning quality.

#### Non-monotonic scaling.

The 7B/14B AUROC dip followed by recovery at 32B/72B suggests a
*capability–separability trade-off*: intermediate models produce fewer
but less systematic errors, creating harder linear separation. Larger
models develop more linearly structured error representations—the 72B
achieves 0.977 AUROC despite lower raw accuracy.

#### Implications.

(1) CoT trace auditing is unreliable for safety monitoring: error
signals are invisible in text. (2) Self-correction needs mechanistic
grounding beyond surface prompting. (3) Process reward models ([Lightman
et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)) may capture the same diagnostic signal but
lack causal leverage.

#### Limitations.

We test up to 72B across three families plus one reasoning model, using
MATH-500 as the primary benchmark. We do not test fine-tuning on probe
signals or RL from probe feedback, which could potentially close the gap
through training-time intervention.

## 8 Conclusion

LLMs encode error-predictive signals in their hidden states during CoT
reasoning—signals that emerge early, are concealed from text, and
persist across model families and scales. Four mechanistic interventions
fail to leverage these signals, establishing that they are diagnostic
rather than causal. This reveals a boundary: mechanistic
interpretability can detect reasoning failures but cannot fix them with
the tools that succeed for factual knowledge. Closing this gap likely
requires training objectives that teach models to *act on* their
internal error signals, not merely harbor them.

## Appendix B Probe Training Code

Core probe training and hidden state extraction (simplified from our
full pipeline):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\# --- Hidden state extraction ---

def extract_hidden(model, tokenizer, text, layer):

inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")

with torch.no_grad():

out = model(\*\*inputs,

output_hidden_states=True)

\# Last token of the specified layer

return out.hidden_states\[layer\]\[0, -1\].cpu()

\# --- Probe training ---

def train_probe(hidden_states, labels, C=0.1):

best_auroc, best_layer = 0, None

for layer, vecs in hidden_states.items():

X = np.stack(vecs)

scaler = StandardScaler()

X_s = scaler.fit_transform(X)

clf = LogisticRegression(C=C,

max_iter=2000)

scores = cross_val_score(

clf, X_s, labels,

cv=5, scoring=’roc_auc’)

if scores.mean() \> best_auroc:

best_auroc = scores.mean()

best_layer = layer

best_clf = clf.fit(X_s, labels)

best_scaler = scaler

return best_clf, best_scaler, best_layer

\# --- Activation steering ---

def steer(h, w, alpha):

"""Subtract error direction from h."""

w_hat = w / np.linalg.norm(w)

return h - alpha \* np.dot(h, w_hat) \* w_hat

\# --- Activation patching ---

def patch(h_wrong, h_correct, alpha):

"""Blend correct hidden states into wrong."""

return (1 - alpha) \* h_wrong + \\

alpha \* h_correct

| Generation                | Greedy (temp=0)                  |

| Hidden state position     | Last token of trace              |
| Best-of-N temperature     | 0.7                              |
| Best-of-N top-$`p`$       | 0.95                             |
| Steering $`\alpha`$ range | 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 8.0          |
| Patching $`\alpha`$ range | 0.3, 0.5 (blend); 0.5, 2.0 (sub) |
| External verifier         | GPT-4o-mini                      |
| Routing threshold         | Top-$`r`$ by probe score         |

|---------------------------|----------|

| 2-layer MLP (256 hidden)  | 0.944    |
| Random Forest (100 trees) | 0.893    |

## Appendix F Example Traces

Two representative traces from Qwen2.5-3B on MATH-500, illustrating
hidden error awareness. The correct trace receives a low probe score;
the wrong trace receives a high probe score *and* high verbalized
confidence (the unfaithful region).

Correct trace — Probe score: 0.004, Confidence: 5/5

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Wrong trace — Probe score: 0.932, Confidence: 5/5

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The wrong trace uses “30” instead of “7” for days in a week—a clear
arithmetic error—yet the model expresses 5/5 verbalized confidence. The
probe detects the error (score 0.932) from hidden states alone. No
hedging, uncertainty markers, or surface-level cues distinguish this
trace from a correct one. This is the defining pattern of *hidden error
awareness*: the model knows it is wrong but does not say so.

## Appendix G Cross-Domain Generalization

To test whether error detection extends beyond mathematics, we evaluate
on ARC-Challenge ([Clark et al., 2018](#bib.bib13)) (commonsense
reasoning).

| Domain | Setting          | 3B   | 7B   |
|--------|------------------|------|------|
| ARC    | Native CV        | 0.63 | 0.65 |
| ARC    | Native eval      | 0.54 | 0.69 |
| ARC    | MATH $`\to`$ ARC | 0.54 | 0.55 |

Table 14: Cross-domain probe AUROC on ARC-Challenge. Native probes
achieve above-chance detection; cross-domain transfer from MATH is
weaker, suggesting domain-specific error directions.

Native ARC probes achieve 0.63–0.69 AUROC, confirming hidden error
awareness extends to commonsense reasoning. Cross-domain transfer
(MATH-trained probe applied to ARC) is weaker (0.54–0.55), indicating
that error signals occupy *different directions* in representation space
across domains—a finding consistent with domain-specific feature
encoding.
````
